title: Sedimentation equilibrium and gravity dependent stiffness coefficients of colloidal hard-spheres
authors: Luis G. MacDowell, Eva G. Noya
abstract: Spherical colloids with harsh repulsive forces have long been used as experimental analogs of the hard sphere model, with demonstrated good agreement with computer simulations for bulk and structural properties of the fluid, glass and crystal phases. However, an enigmatic discrepancy remains for the crystal-melt stiffness coefficient. Here we perform computer simulations of colloidal hard spheres under tunable buoyant mass and show that the long-standing discrepancy can be traced to a hitherto unrecognized gravity dependent contribution of the stiffness coefficient. This effect is one practical realization of a more general result for the external field dependence of stiffness coefficients of arbitrary interfaces.
summary: This work investigates the interfacial properties of colloidal hard spheres under gravity, focusing on a discrepancy in the crystal-melt stiffness coefficient. Using computer simulations, the authors demonstrate that this missing physics arises from an explicit, previously overlooked dependence of the stiffness coefficient on the external gravitational field. This provides a general result for how external fields affect interface thermodynamics.
main_problem: The study addresses an enigmatic discrepancy concerning the crystal-melt stiffness coefficient of colloidal hard spheres, particularly when external gravity is considered.
main_result: The authors show that this long-standing discrepancy can be traced to a previously unrecognized, explicit dependence of the interfacial stiffness coefficient on the applied gravitational field.
method: Computer simulations (Monte Carlo) are used to calculate density profiles and analyze the capillary wave spectrum at fluid-crystal interfaces under tunable buoyant mass and gravity.
model_or_system: The system modeled is colloidal hard spheres, which serve as an experimental analog for studying bulk and interfacial properties of simple fluids undergoing phase transitions into crystalline solids.
key_observables: Interfacial stiffness coefficient ($	ilde{\gamma}$), density profiles ($ho(z)$), pressure tensor components ($P_{zz}, P_{xx}, P_{yy}$), and the mean squared amplitude of surface Fourier modes ($\langle h^2_q angle$).
important_parameters: Buoyant mass, external gravity ($	ilde{G}$), reduced temperature/pressure parameters (e.g., $ eta p\sigma^3 = 11.65$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on relating interfacial properties to the capillary wave spectrum and uses simplified ansätze for density profiles in some theoretical derivations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate density and pressure profiles showing stratification due to gravity, and compare simulated vs. fitted capillary wave spectra across varying gravity strengths ($	ilde{G}$).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical model (colloidal hard spheres) and identifying the discrepancy, through detailed simulation analysis of equilibrium states under gravity, culminating in deriving the functional form showing $	ilde{\gamma}$'s dependence on $	ilde{G}$.
why_interesting: While focused on classical colloidal systems, the rigorous treatment of external field effects (gravity) modifying fundamental thermodynamic coefficients like stiffness is relevant to understanding non-equilibrium or externally driven many-body dynamics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Pressure and density profiles. The black and orange lines are the zz component of the pressure tensor by IK and MOP methods, which overlap one on top of the other. The red and blue are xx and yy components, which also overlap. Oscillations about the zz component suggest equilibrium. The system always crystallizes very close to the intersection of pzz(z) with the equilibrium coexistence pressure, as displayed by the dashed black line in the figures for βpσ3 = 11.65, the estimated coexistence pressure of PHS.

FIG. 2. Capillary wave spectrum for interfaces under gravity. Results are shown for surface fluctuations on the (100) interface (left) and the (110) interface along the [001] direction (right), with ˜G = 0 (green), ˜G = 0.75 (blue) and ˜G = 1.50 (red). The symbols are average simulation results from four independent runs. The lines are fits to the 20 first wave-vectors to Eq.6. For ease of view, the results for ˜G = 0.75 and ˜G = 1.5 are shifted by 0.25 and 0.50 along the y axis, respectively.

FIG. 3. Coefficients of the spectrum of fluctuations as obtained form simulation. Results for the (100)[001] direction are shown as circles, while those for the (100)[001] direction are shown as squares. For g′′, the line corresponds to the prediction g′′ = ∆ρ ˜G from capillary wave theory with no fitting parameters. For the other figures, lines are linear fits to the data. The middle panel also shows stiffness coefficients in zero gravity obtained from Ref.45 (red diamons), Ref.47 (violet triangles up) and Ref.51 (orange triangles down).

FIG. 4. Comparison of density profiles for HS and p-HS. Bluelines are density profiles from the pseudo-Hard Spheres, simulated by MD with Lammps. Green lines are results for HS, simulated with MC. The results do not show any difference in the scale of the plot.
